analysis.title: Weekly Macro Brief
key_insights: Citi's Jim McCormick sees value, inflation and fiscal policy all pointing to higher UST yields. USTs remain the main G10 bond to sell, with a growing bias toward UST steepeners.

The 10y UST yield rose 27bps in the past week, one of the biggest one-week rises in recent years. Drivers were a hot US CPI and a speech by Fed Governor Waller implying a 50bps hike was on the table for the December FOMC.
Two weeks ago the S&P 500 and oil had their largest declines since the pandemic, triggered by large Democratic wins in the US midterm elections.

Value: none of the four UST valuation measures McCormick tracks is bullish. The current 10y yield (5.14%) is at the low end of its sustainable range, the synthetic 10y real yield says the same, US nominal GDP is running above 10y yields, and the fundamental term premia model implies more upside adjustment. Only relative pricing against equities is bullish USTs, and that needs a view that equity weakness will persist.

Inflation: y/y core PCE has not been below 2% since February 2021. The October data will likely show core PCE rising from 2.9% to 3.2% this year, with little sign of sub-3% well into 2027, after methodological changes meant to show a tamer trend. Upstream price measures in tech (China PPI, Japan export prices) are also not encouraging.

Core PCE has been stuck near 3% for nearly three years while oil traded between $60 and $120, so the drop in energy prices is not a reason to ignore core inflation. McCormick says USD inflation markets need to reprice, and last week may have been the start.

Fiscal: the 2025 US deficit improvement has reversed in 2026, with higher spending the biggest driver. After the midterms, the Administration wants more defense spending and the Democratic Congress wants healthcare relief, so 2027 is unlikely to improve. The US has the worst structural fiscal position of any DM country but still faces limited bond market pressure, unlike France and Belgium.

Fed credibility: the 2s10s curve is the flattest of any major market, breakevens are below pre-Iran-conflict levels and the trade-weighted dollar is higher. Citi's dollar debasement basket closed at its lowest since mid-2025, helped by another drop in gold. McCormick calls these credibility gains excessive.

After the latest CPI, the Fed scores second most hawkish on Citi's central bank dual-mandate score, behind the BOJ. The Fed has delivered only 25bps of hikes this year and the market prices 80bps more. Only the SNB and Norges Bank have meaningfully more dovish pricing.

McCormick thinks a 50bps December hike is highly unlikely. Back-to-back December/January hikes would help but not convince. The Fed is unlikely to hike enough to bring down inflation because it wants to avoid higher unemployment, so he expects a steeper curve and higher breakevens, and a weaker dollar. Stay short USTs cross-market and use the recent flattening to rebuild steepeners.

UK: monthly GDP beat again, with the y/y trend at its fastest since 2022. A December BOE hike is priced at 75% and moves higher if next week's CPI and labor data are firm. Trades: paid front BOE meetings and long 30y gilts vs 10y UST.

Japan: a December BOJ hike looks nearly certain and is not fully priced. The BoJ Summary of Opinions was hawkish, Fed tightening pricing is higher and USD/JPY is rising. Trades: paid front BOJ meetings and 5s30s JGB flattener. Q3 GDP is reported early next week.

Euro area: Spain's De Cos is reportedly in pole position for ECB President, which would add dovish pricing to the front end. Weak growth with little inflation pass-through means one more ECB hike, likely in December, while three hikes are priced. France may already be in recession. Trade: receive front-end EUR rates.

Australia: long AUD 10y bonds vs USTs remains a favorite structural trade. The AUD-US 10y spread is at its lowest in over a year, and McCormick sees at least 50bps left. Markets begin to price cuts only from late 2027. Next week's employment and wage data will inform whether the RBA hiking cycle is done.

McCormick's broad G10 duration view is neutral, though he sees many trades within fixed income. Chinese clients showed interest in non-USD fixed income (France, Australia, Brazil). He thinks rapid de-dollarisation is unlikely, though some diversification away from USTs is inevitable.

risk_factors: A 50bps December Fed hike or a sustained equity decline could support USTs.
Firm UK CPI and labor data would raise BOE hike pricing further, softer data would hurt the BOE trade.
Strong Australian wage and employment data could keep the RBA hiking.
A repricing in USD inflation markets is still needed. A Fed that hikes too little risks higher breakevens and a weaker dollar.
Bond market pressure on the US fiscal position has been limited so far.

tension_points.bull_case: The market prices a highly credible Fed reaction function, with the flattest 2s10s curve of any major market, breakevens below pre-Iran-conflict levels and a stronger trade-weighted dollar.
tension_points.bear_case: The Fed has delivered only 25bps of hikes while ranking second most hawkish on Citi's dual-mandate score, and is unlikely to hike enough to bring down inflation because it wants to avoid higher unemployment, implying a steeper curve, higher breakevens and a weaker dollar.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 50bps December hike or back-to-back December/January hikes would help credibility, though Citi calls the 50bps move highly unlikely.
